chapters.title: Chapter 6: Taxes on Getting Money Out of the Company

lessons.title: Salary, Dividend or Buyback: What Each Route Really Costs a Founder

body.text: A founder who owns the whole company still cannot simply take money from it. Every rupee that moves from the company's account to yours travels through one of a few named routes, and they are taxed very differently. Choosing the route is the single largest personal tax decision most business owners ever make.

children.text: Chapter 1 showed why a company's profit is not yours. This lesson works out what it costs to make it yours. The three main routes are salary, dividend and buyback, and their tax treatment differs enough that the same ₹50 lakh of company profit can leave you with anything from about ₹30 lakh to about ₹39 lakh.

body.caption: The three main routes, side by side

cells: Salary, at slab rates, after the standard deduction
No. Paid out of profit already taxed
Income from other sources, at slab rates
No. Paid out of post-tax reserves
Rent, if the company uses property you own
Income from house property, with a standard deduction
Interest, if you have lent money to the company

body.text: Look down the second column. Salary, rent and interest are deductible, so the company never pays corporate tax on that money. Dividend and buyback come out of profit that has already borne 25.168%. That single difference drives almost everything that follows.

children.text: ₹50 Lakh of Profit, Three Ways Out

A founder owns a profitable private limited company in the concessional regime under section 200 [old 115BAA]. The company has ₹50,00,000 of pre-tax profit it can move to her this year. She has no other income and is taxed under the default personal regime in section 202 [old 115BAC]. For the buyback route, assume her shares cost ₹1,00,000 and have been held for more than two years.

body.caption: Where ₹50,00,000 of pre-tax profit ends up

cells: Nil, the whole amount is deductible

body.title: What the founder actually keeps, from ₹50,00,000 of company profit
Show me the math for all three routes

children.text: The company deducts the full ₹50,00,000 as an expense, so no corporate tax arises on it. In her hands, the ₹75,000 standard deduction leaves ₹49,25,000 taxable. Under the section 202 slabs, the first ₹24,00,000 produces ₹3,00,000 of tax, and the remaining ₹25,25,000 is taxed at 30%, which is ₹7,57,500. Tax before cess is ₹10,57,500, and 4% cess takes it to ₹10,99,800. Her total income stays below ₹50,00,000, so no surcharge applies.

The company pays 25.168% on ₹50,00,000, or ₹12,58,400, leaving ₹37,41,600 to distribute. There is no standard deduction against dividend income, so the whole amount is taxable: ₹3,00,000 on the first ₹24,00,000, then ₹13,41,600 at 30%, which is ₹4,02,480. With 4% cess, her tax is ₹7,30,579. The company also deducts 10% TDS when paying, which she adjusts against this liability.

Corporate tax is the same ₹12,58,400, because a buyback is paid out of reserves that have already been taxed. The ₹37,41,600 she receives is capital gains, reduced by the ₹1,00,000 cost of the shares tendered, leaving a gain of ₹36,41,600. As a long-term gain on unlisted shares it is taxed at 12.5%, or ₹4,55,200, and 4% cess takes it to ₹4,73,408.
Provident fund, professional tax and the cost of running each route are ignored throughout, as is the additional levy that applies to promoters on a buyback, which is covered below.

body.label: Why salary wins on arithmetic
body.value: It is the only deductible route
body.context: Dividend and buyback both travel through corporate tax first. Salary does not, which is worth ₹12,58,400 on ₹50,00,000 before a single rupee of personal tax is computed.

body.text: That does not make salary the automatic answer. It must be genuine remuneration for work actually done, supported by a board resolution, an employment agreement and monthly TDS. A founder who is not involved in operations cannot draw a large salary for appearing on the cap table, and an excessive payment can be challenged as unreasonable and disallowed, leaving you with the worst of both worlds: tax at slab in your hands and no deduction for the company.

body.title: Quick Check: Which Route Reduces Company Tax?
body.question: A company wants to transfer value to its founder. Which of these reduces the company's own taxable income?
options: Paying a market-rate salary for the founder's executive role
Buying back some of the founder's shares
Issuing bonus shares to the founder
body.explanation: Only salary is a deductible business expense. Dividends and buybacks are appropriations of profit already taxed at 25.168%, and bonus shares transfer no money at all, they simply split the same ownership into more pieces. Rent and interest paid to a founder are also deductible, provided they are at commercial rates and properly documented.

children.text: Buyback Changed Twice in Two Years

events.title: The company paid
events.description: A buyback tax was levied on the company itself, and the amount received was exempt in the shareholder's hands.

events.title: Shifted to the shareholder as dividend
events.description: The entire buyback consideration became taxable in the shareholder's hands as deemed dividend, at slab rates, with no deduction for the cost of the shares. The cost was allowed separately as a capital loss.

events.title: Restored to capital gains
events.description: The Finance Act, 2026 reversed the dividend treatment. Buyback consideration is now taxed as capital gains, computed as consideration less cost of acquisition, with an additional levy on promoters.

body.text: The promoter levy matters for exactly the readers of this lesson. Where a buyback is carried out under the Companies Act buyback provisions, promoters pay an additional charge on top of normal capital gains tax, with a further surcharge on that additional tax. Reported effective rates for promoters run far above the headline 12.5%, which substantially narrows the advantage over a dividend. Before planning any buyback from founder shareholdings, get the current rates confirmed by your adviser, because this is the most recently changed rule in this entire course.

body.title: Try It: The Dividend Route
body.prompt: A company in the concessional regime has ₹20,00,000 of pre-tax profit that it wants to pay out as dividend. After corporate tax at 25.168%, how much is available to distribute? Answer in rupees.
body.explanation: Corporate tax is ₹20,00,000 × 25.168%, which is ₹5,03,360, leaving ₹14,96,640 to distribute. The shareholder then pays tax on that ₹14,96,640 at their own slab rate, with the company deducting 10% TDS when it pays. A dividend is therefore taxed twice by design, once in the company and once in the shareholder's hands.

body.caption: Tax is not the only constraint

cells: Board approval, an employment agreement, and for public companies statutory limits on managerial remuneration
Payable only out of profits or free reserves, declared for a whole class of shares, so every shareholder of that class participates proportionately
Limits on how much can be bought back and how often, a debt to capital test, shareholder approval, and a cooling period before the next buyback
Loan to a director or shareholder
Restricted under company law, and a loan to a substantial shareholder can be taxed as deemed dividend

body.text: The dividend rule catches founders with investors. A dividend cannot be paid to you alone. Every holder of that class of shares receives their proportion, so declaring ₹1 crore to take ₹60 lakh for yourself means ₹40 lakh leaves for your investors too. Salary, rent and interest are specific to you. That difference often decides the route long before tax rates do.

body.title: Scenario: The Founder Who Needs ₹1 Crore
body.scenario: A founder owns 70% of a profitable Chennai software company, with a venture fund holding the rest. She needs about ₹1 crore for a house purchase. She currently draws a modest salary of ₹18 lakh a year, well below what a chief executive of that company would command. The company has ₹4 crore of accumulated reserves and strong cash flow.
body.prompt: How should she structure this, and what should she avoid?
body.modelAnswer: Start with what is already available and underused. Her salary is below market for the role, so raising it to a defensible market level is the cheapest route, because every rupee is deductible for the company and she is taxed only once. That correction should be made prospectively, with a board resolution, a revised employment agreement and benchmarking evidence, not backdated to create a lump sum. If she also owns property the company occupies, or has lent it money, market rent and reasonable interest are similarly deductible and specific to her. Dividend is the obvious next lever but an expensive one here for two reasons: the money has already borne 25.168% corporate tax, and because dividends go to a whole class of shares, paying herself ₹1 crore means roughly ₹43 lakh also leaving to the fund, which the fund may not even want. A buyback of some of her shares would be capital gains rather than dividend from 1 April 2026, but the additional promoter levy narrows that advantage considerably, and a buyback from a founder in a venture-backed company also shifts the cap table and will need investor consent under the shareholders agreement. What she must not do is take the money as a loan from the company and plan to sort it out later. That is restricted under company law and can be taxed as deemed dividend in her hands, producing the tax of the dividend route with none of the legitimacy. The practical answer is a mix: correct the salary now, use rent or interest if those assets exist, take a dividend for the balance if the timing cannot wait, and price the buyback option properly with her adviser before assuming it is cheaper.

body.title: Fill in the Blank: Dividend Withholding
body.textWithBlank: When a company pays a dividend to a resident individual shareholder above the prescribed threshold, it must deduct TDS at ___ percent.
body.explanation: Ten percent, under section 393 [old 194]. That is a withholding, not the final tax: the shareholder adds the gross dividend to total income, pays at their slab rate, and claims the TDS as credit. A founder in the 30% bracket will therefore owe more than the 10% already deducted, which is why dividends need to be built into advance tax estimates.

body.title: Documentation That Makes Each Route Defensible
steps: Salary: board resolution, employment agreement, evidence of the role performed, monthly TDS and payslips
Rent: a registered or written lease at market rent, proof the space is actually used, TDS on rent
Interest: a loan agreement, a commercial rate, TDS on the interest paid
Dividend: board and shareholder approvals, payment to all holders of the class, TDS deducted and deposited
Buyback: shareholder approval, compliance with company law limits, valuation support, and current advice on the promoter levy
Every route: pay through the bank, never in cash, and record it in the year it is actually paid
Build expected dividend and salary into your personal advance tax estimate before 15 June each year

cards.definition: A payment such as salary, rent or interest that reduces the company's taxable income, so the money is taxed only in your hands.
A payment such as dividend or buyback made from profit already taxed in the company, producing two layers of tax.
TDS on salary, deducted monthly at the employee's average rate for the year.
TDS on dividend, at 10% above the prescribed threshold, adjusted against the shareholder's final liability.
The company purchasing its own shares from a shareholder. Taxed as capital gains from 1 April 2026, with an additional levy on promoters.
A loan or advance from a closely held company to a substantial shareholder, taxed as though a dividend had been declared.
Accumulated profits available for distribution, which limit how much a company can pay as dividend or use for a buyback.

points: Salary, rent and interest are deductible for the company, so that money bears only one layer of tax
Dividend and buyback come out of profit already taxed at 25.168%, which is why they cost more overall
On ₹50,00,000 of pre-tax profit, the salary route left about ₹39 lakh in hand against about ₹30 lakh for a dividend
Salary must be genuine, reasonable and documented, or it is disallowed and taxed anyway
Buyback moved from a company-level tax to deemed dividend in October 2024, and to capital gains from 1 April 2026, with an additional levy on promoters
A dividend must go to every shareholder of the class, so it is an expensive way for one founder to extract cash in an investor-backed company
Taking money as a loan from your own company is restricted and risks being taxed as deemed dividend

body.text: This lesson is for educational purposes only and does not constitute tax, legal or investment advice. Section references reflect the Income-tax Act, 2025 as understood at the time of writing, with the corresponding 1961 Act section shown in brackets. Buyback taxation changed with effect from 1 April 2026 and the additional levy on promoters is new, so confirm the current rates and conditions with a qualified chartered accountant and company secretary before structuring any extraction of funds from your company.
